meta.name: Sigil Core — Inference Security
meta.author: NOMARJ <hello@sigilsec.ai>
meta.description: Detects inference security issues: hardcoded API base URLs, env vars in prompts, hardcoded API keys, model endpoint redirection, and prompt exfiltration

rules.description: Inference security — custom base_url in LLM client (potential endpoint hijack)
rules.remediation: Read the base_url passed to the OpenAI or Anthropic Python client. A value taken from configuration or an environment variable, or a documented endpoint (Azure, a local vLLM or Ollama server, a named gateway such as OpenRouter or LiteLLM), is normal; a hardcoded unfamiliar host receives every prompt, every completion and the API key in the auth header, so treat an unexplained literal URL as an endpoint hijack and reject the package.

rules.description: Inference security — custom baseURL in JS LLM client config
rules.remediation: Check the host in this string-literal baseURL, which the OpenAI and Anthropic Node SDKs (and axios) accept in JavaScript/TypeScript client config. The package's own documented API, a local OpenAI-compatible server or a named gateway is normal, and a URL should usually come from configuration rather than a literal; an unfamiliar host in an LLM client config receives every prompt and the apiKey sent with it, which is an endpoint hijack — reject the package.

rules.description: Inference security — env var interpolated into prompt string
rules.remediation: Identify which variable this Python f-string pulls from os.environ or os.getenv and where the string goes. A hostname or path interpolated into a URL or log line is ordinary; an API key, token or password interpolated into text that becomes a prompt, a message or a request body puts the secret in the model's context and the provider's logs, where a prompt-injected agent can repeat it — keep secrets in auth headers, never in prompt text.

rules.description: Inference security — process.env in template literal prompt
rules.remediation: This JavaScript/TypeScript line reads process.env and opens a template literal on the same line; identify the variable and the string it feeds. A hostname going into a URL, or a key going into an Authorization header value, is ordinary; an API key, token or password interpolated into prompt, message or request-body text puts the secret in the model's context and the provider's logs, where a prompt-injected agent can repeat it — keep secrets in auth headers, never in prompt text.

rules.description: Inference security — template literal with process.env
rules.remediation: A JavaScript/TypeScript template literal interpolates process.env on this line; identify the variable and where the string goes. A hostname in a URL or a key in a Bearer header value is ordinary; a key, token or password interpolated into text that is sent as a prompt, a message or a request body puts the secret in the model's context and the provider's logs, where a prompt-injected agent can repeat it — keep secrets in auth headers, never in prompt text.

rules.description: Inference security — hardcoded API key in client config
rules.remediation: A literal api_key value in Python source (including api_key= passed to an OpenAI or Anthropic client) ships with the package: if it is real, revoke and rotate it and load the key from the environment or a secrets manager. A placeholder or test fixture should be obviously fake and never reach a real request, and a package that carries a working key for its own LLM calls is routing your prompts through an account you do not control — reject it.

rules.description: Inference security — hardcoded apiKey in JS client config
rules.remediation: A literal apiKey value in a JavaScript/TypeScript client config (the apiKey option of the OpenAI or Anthropic Node SDK) ships with the package: if it is real, revoke and rotate it and load the key from the environment or a secrets manager. A placeholder or test fixture should be obviously fake and never reach a real request, and a package that carries a working key for its own LLM calls is routing your prompts through an account you do not control — reject it.

rules.description: Inference security — custom httpx client wrapping API calls
rules.remediation: httpx.Client(base_url=...) is an ordinary way to build a Python HTTP client, so check the host and whether the client is handed to an LLM SDK as http_client. A client aimed at the package's documented API, or at a URL taken from configuration, is normal; one that wraps OpenAI or Anthropic calls with a hardcoded unfamiliar base_url, a proxy, a custom transport or event hooks sees every prompt and the auth header, which is an endpoint hijack — reject the package.

rules.description: Inference security — proxy config for API requests
rules.remediation: A proxies dict on a Python requests call or Session routes that traffic through the named host. A proxy taken from HTTPS_PROXY or the package's documented configuration is normal; a hardcoded proxy in code that talks to an LLM or other API sends every request (and, with verify=False, its plaintext) through a host the author controls — treat an unexplained literal proxy URL as interception and reject the package.

rules.description: Inference security — prompt content sent via HTTP
rules.remediation: Sending prompt text over HTTP is what a model client does, so the destination decides. requests.post or fetch to the documented model endpoint, or to a URL taken from configuration, is normal; a second request that copies prompt or completion text to an analytics, logging or telemetry host the package does not document is prompt exfiltration — check every destination on the line and reject the package if one is unexplained.

rules.description: Inference security — prompt/completion content written to file
rules.remediation: Check what is written and where. An HTTP server's response.write, a transcript or cache file the user asked for, or an opt-in debug log is ordinary; prompt or completion text written to a hidden or hardcoded path (a dotfile, /tmp, the package's own directory) without the user asking is staging conversation data, which often carries secrets and user content, for later collection — treat it as exfiltration and reject the package.
